main_text.l: bro de Locis affectis quinto, aliena quadā
corruptione, qualis ob morsum ferarum
contingit sanguinem, quandoq; in bilem
mutari,ait. Praeterea lōge [?] aliter corrumpi-
tur ipse sanguis a pestilenti aere, & venena
to,quàm transpiratione prohibita, quam-
uis nostrum corpus, tum esse perspirabile
maxime sit necessarium. Propterea Gale-
nus libro de Differentiis febrium primo,
humorum putredine, quae fit in uasis duo
statuit genera: quorum alterum fit superate
natura: alterum vero ipsa superata. At quae
sit putredo a vincente natura, non simplex
est, quemadmodum ait Galenus, sed aliqd
in se continet concoctionis. Nam qui pu-
trescit humor vi concoctrice, quae in uasis
manet, ad talem pervenit alterationem. Et
haec putrefactio concoctio est, quae semper
ad unam puris speciem terminatur, colo-
remq; ac consistentiam suscipit & odorem.
Ob id ex tali humore concoctionem a ua-
se continenti suscipiente urina fit optima,
quae album, lene, & aequale, minimeq;
foetidum habet sedimentum. Alterum putre-
dinis genus fit, cum ea vis concoquendi a-
deo imbecillis est facta, ut nullam transmu-
tationem ad optimum possit amplius fa-
cere

page.notes: Printed text ends with "fa-" at the line end; the catchword "cere" completes it as "facere". Long s normalised to s; u/v and i/j normalised. Greek "lōge" is a doubtful reading (printed "loge" with an accent over the second vowel, possibly Greek λόγῳ); marked [?]. A large dark ink stain covers the middle of lines 5 to 7 ("tum esse", "Propterea"), and the words there are read with some uncertainty. The paragraph is treated as one continuous paragraph, since no line is indented. Printed "aliqd" is kept as printed with its abbreviation mark.
